newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia bond yields up as Fed policy cycle turns.
newsitem.headline: Australia bond yields up as Fed policy cycle turns.

text.p: Australian bond yields finished higher in the aftermath of Tuesday's U.S. interest rate hike, but the market took the move pretty much in its stride and had established a trading range shortly after the opening.

The endorsement of a 25 basis point rise by the Federal Open Market Committee in the U.S. Fed funds rate to 5.50 percent had been widely expected, and was seen having no impact on Reserve Bank policy, economists said.
However, speculation is already mounting as to when the Fed will move again.

"Slowing the U.S. will take more tightenings, but the cycle will not be as prolonged as in previous episodes," said John Edwards, chief economist at HSBC Markets, who expected a further 25 basis point rate rise on May 20 and perhaps another in July.

In a statement following the FOMC meeting, the Fed said its action was taken in the light of persisting strength in demand, which is progressively increasing the risk of inflationary imbalances developing in the economy.
Economists at ANZ Securities expect the next U.S. rate hike to be in July, and say such expectations will probably see U.S. bond yields put under further upward pressue.

"We are targetting a 7.25 percent (U.S.) 30-year bond yield as the peak, with the 10-year bond at 7.0 percent. The peak should probably occur around the time of the next rate increase in July," ANZ Securities said in a report.
The U.S. 10-year bond was at 6.77 percent and the 30-year at 6.97 percent in Tokyo trading.

The local benchmark November 2006 bond spiked back through 8.0 percent, but analysts see scope for the domestic debt to outperform the U.S. given Australia's higher unemployment, propects for further fiscal tightening in May and expectations that inflation data next month will confirm the benign outlook.
"All these factors mean that there is no chance the Reserve Bank of Australia will follow the Fed at its board meeting next Tuesday," HSBC's Edwards added.

Treasurer Peter Costello also told parliament that the local inflation outlook remained the key to Australian monetary policy, noting that underlying rate, currently at 2.1 percent, is well within the RBA's 2.0-3.0 percent target.
"We see a continuing low inflation, low interest rate environment...," Costello added.

The Australian/U.S. 10-year yield spread see-sawed around Tuesday's local closing level for most of the day. Analysts believe 130 b.p. should be the top for the market in the current environment. Canadian bonds ended Tuesday little change on the Fed move, while New Zealand debt took the news negatively.
